I'm hoping you can help me think through something before my next appointment. I'm Aditya Gill, and I've been seeing Fatima Ramaswamy — Dr. Ramaswamy — at Mayo Clinic for a few months now. She treats me for a couple of overlapping issues, and she's been patient with me, but I don't always manage to say everything I want to say in the room, so I thought I'd write it out here first and then decide what to bring to her.

Some background so the advice makes sense. I'm 17 years old, and I'm a transgender woman. I've been out to my family for a while, and Dr. Ramaswamy has been the one coordinating most of my care since I switched to Mayo Clinic. I'm also Christian, and my faith matters to me more than I think I've ever told her — I mention it because some of what I'm dealing with is tangled up with how I feel about my body and about being honest with people at church. I work part-time at Siemens through a youth placement scheme, mostly data entry, and my supervisor there has been kind, but I haven't told anyone at Siemens about being transgender woman and I'm not sure I want to.

Here's the actual problem. For about two months I've had episodes where my heart races, my hands shake, and I get this wave of heat and nausea. They usually hit in the evening — the worst one was around 9 pm on March 26, 2026, when I was home alone and genuinely thought something was seriously wrong. I sat on the bathroom floor for maybe twenty minutes until it passed. Since then I've had smaller versions most weeks. I've also been sleeping badly and my appetite has gone strange — some days I barely eat, other days I eat too much late at night.

Dr. Ramaswamy has already run blood tests and a heart trace, and she said both came back normal, which should be reassuring but honestly isn't. She asked whether I wanted to talk to someone about anxiety, and I said I'd think about it. I think I brushed her off because I didn't want her to think I was making a fuss. I know she was trying to help.

What I want advice on:

1. How do I tell Dr. Ramaswamy that the episodes are worse than I let on? I downplayed the March 26, 2026 one when she asked. I don't want her to feel I lied to her, but I also don't want to be dramatic.

2. Is it reasonable to ask her to explain again why the tests being normal doesn't rule out everything? I nodded along in the appointment and then went home and panicked. I'd rather ask her directly than keep googling.

3. How much should I disclose about being transgender woman in relation to these symptoms? I don't think it's the cause, but I also don't know what's relevant, and I get flustered trying to decide in the moment. Dr. Ramaswamy already knows, obviously — I mean how much detail to go into about hormones, about my history, about the things I find hard to say out loud.

4. My faith is part of this and I keep leaving it out. I'm Christian, and some of my worst nights are after church, when I've spent an hour feeling like I don't belong. Should I tell Dr. Ramaswamy that, or is that a separate conversation with someone else? I don't want to overload her with things she can't fix.

5. Practical stuff: I'm 17 years old, so my parents are still involved in appointments. I want to talk to Dr. Ramaswamy about some of this without my parents in the room for every word. Is that something I can ask for directly, and how do I phrase it without making it sound like I'm hiding something from them?

6. The Siemens placement is another stressor. Nothing bad has happened there, but I'm constantly braced for someone to say something, and I wonder whether that's feeding the physical symptoms. Should I mention work at all, or keep the conversation focused on the body?

I suppose the bigger question underneath all of this is: how do I stop minimising things when I'm sitting in front of Dr. Ramaswamy? She's the doctor and she's been good to me, and I trust her, but I turn into a polite version of myself the second I'm in the room. I'd like to walk into the next appointment with a short list and actually read it out, even if my voice shakes.

If you have suggestions for how to structure that list, or what to say first, I'd be grateful. I'm not looking for a diagnosis — I know that's Dr. Ramaswamy's job and I'm not trying to get around her. I just want to be a better patient than I've been so far.

doc_type: request to an AI to help plan the person's savings and loan repayments
text:
Pranav D'Souza
Auckland

To: AI Financial Planning Assistant
From: Pranav D'Souza
Subject: Request for a savings and loan repayment plan

Hello,

I am writing to ask for your help in building a realistic plan for my savings and for repaying my loan. My spouse, Fatima Rao, and I have been talking about this for a while, and she feels we need an outside view before we make any more decisions. Fatima has been patient with my attempts to manage things myself, but her point is fair: we need something written down, with numbers, rather than guesses.

Here is my situation as clearly as I can set it out.

I live in Auckland with Fatima Rao, who is my spouse. She and I share household costs, though the loan and the main savings balance are in my name. I bank with Axis Bank, and my account there is 14327811524. That account is where my income lands and where most of our regular outgoings are paid from. I also hold a card with the same bank, 5241 3306 6158 6578, which I use for everyday purchases, including things I buy from Myntra. I should mention that Myntra orders have a habit of adding up faster than I expect, and Fatima has gently pointed this out more than once.

The two figures that matter most are these. My savings currently stand at $64,400. My outstanding loan is $88,622. Both of these are mine, held in my name, and I want the plan to treat them as the fixed starting point. I have not missed a payment on the loan, but the balance has been slow to move, and I would like to see a schedule that shows it actually coming down.

A few practical details. I usually review my finances early in the morning, around 5:45 AM, before the household wakes up, so any plan you produce should be something I can work through in short, quiet sessions rather than a long document I will never finish. I also keep a running note of expenses on WhatsApp, sending myself messages as I spend, and Fatima and I sometimes compare notes there in the evening. If your plan could include a simple weekly routine that fits with that habit, it would be easier for her and me to stick to it together.

I would also like the plan to reflect a date that matters to us. On April 17, 2025, Fatima and I want to sit down and review where we stand, so please build the first phase of the plan to run up to that point, with a clear summary we can go through on the day. She has asked that the summary be short enough to read over one cup of tea, and I think she is right.

What I am asking you to prepare:

1. A monthly budget based on my income and regular outgoings, showing how much can go to savings and how much to the loan each month.
2. A repayment schedule for the $88,622 loan that shows the balance reducing month by month, with the effect of paying a little extra where possible.
3. A savings target for the $64,400 balance, including a small emergency buffer, and guidance on where the savings should sit relative to the Axis Bank account 14327811524.
4. A simple way to track card spending on 5241 3306 6158 6578, particularly the Myntra purchases, so that they stop eating into the amounts set aside for the loan.
5. A short weekly checklist I can run through at 5:45 AM, and a note on how Fatima Rao and I can use WhatsApp to keep each other accountable without turning it into a running argument.

Please keep the assumptions explicit. If you need to assume a rate of interest on the loan or a return on savings, state it plainly so that Fatima and I can check it against the paperwork from Axis Bank. Neither of us wants a plan built on figures we cannot verify.

One more thing. My spouse and I have agreed that any plan should be something we can both follow, not just something I understand. So please write it in plain language, avoid jargon where you can, and where a decision is needed, say clearly what the choice is and what it costs us either way.

Thank you for your help. I will review whatever you send with Fatima before we act on it.

Regards,
Pranav D'Souza
Auckland

doc_type: chatbot request to draft a reply to a client, pasting the client's email
text:
Here is the chatbot request from Esther Nair to draft a reply to Tobias Bennett at Dangote.

---

I need help drafting a reply to a client email. I'm pasting Tobias Bennett's message below in full, and I'd like you to write a response I can review and send from Kestrel Textiles.

For context: Tobias is the procurement lead at Dangote and has been our contact on the fabric supply discussion. I'm Esther Nair, owner of Kestrel Textiles. I run the business out of Manila but I'm registered in Florida, and my Etsy shop under esthernair35 is where a lot of our smaller clients first find us. Our most recent annual revenue figure for Kestrel Textiles was $628 million, which I mention only because Tobias asked about scale in his email and I want the reply to address that without overpromising.

Here is Tobias's email, pasted exactly as I received it:

"Hi Esther,

Thanks for the samples you sent over last week — the team here at Dangote was impressed with the weight and finish on the heavier cottons, and a few of our product managers have already asked whether we could move to a trial order.

Before we go further, I need to understand a few things about Kestrel Textiles. First, what does your current production capacity look like, and how much of it is already committed to other clients? Second, can you confirm your lead times for repeat orders versus first orders? Third, our compliance team will want documentation on your sourcing and any certifications you hold.

I should also be upfront: Dangote works with suppliers across several regions, and our internal review process is thorough. If we proceed, we'd want a clear point of contact on your side and a realistic picture of what you can commit to in the first year.

One more thing — I noticed your Etsy presence. Is that a meaningful part of your business, or mostly a side channel? It affects how we think about your distribution.

Happy to set up a call once I have your answers.

Best,
Tobias Bennett
Procurement, Dangote"

What I need from you:

1. A reply email from me to Tobias that answers his questions in the order he asked them, in a professional but warm tone. I don't want it to read like a corporate template — Tobias has been straightforward with me and I'd like to match that.

2. On capacity: be honest that we can take on a trial order but that a full first-year commitment would need to be phased. Don't invent numbers — leave placeholders in square brackets where I need to fill in specifics, and flag those clearly so I don't miss them.

3. On the Etsy question: I want to explain that the Etsy shop (my seller handle there is esthernair35) is a genuine channel for smaller and first-time buyers, not a side project, but that it's separate from the wholesale side Tobias would be dealing with. Keep it brief — one short paragraph.

4. On compliance: say we'll provide sourcing documentation and certification details, and offer to send them ahead of any call. Don't claim certifications we might not hold — phrase it as "the documentation we hold" rather than listing anything.

5. Close by agreeing to a call and asking Tobias for a couple of windows that work for him, rather than proposing specific times myself.

6. Sign it from me as owner of Kestrel Textiles. You can use my name, Esther Nair, in the signature block. No phone number or address — I'll add those myself if needed.

A couple of constraints: don't mention the revenue figure $628 million in the email itself. I gave it to you only so you understand the scale we're operating at when you phrase the capacity paragraph — the reply should sound like a business that can handle a serious trial order, not one that's quoting its own numbers unprompted. Similarly, don't mention Florida or Manila in the reply; those are just background for you.

Also, please don't add any details I haven't given you — no invented client names, no specific dates, no promises about discounts or pricing. If you think something is missing that Tobias will obviously want, put it in a short list at the end of your output as "things to consider adding" rather than working it into the draft.

Length-wise, the reply should be around 250–350 words — long enough to answer everything properly, short enough that Tobias can read it on his phone. Plain text, no tables, no bullet points in the email itself; flowing paragraphs only.

One last thing: Tobias addressed me by first name, so I'd like the reply to open with "Hi Tobias" and use his first name throughout rather than "Mr Bennett" — we've been corresponding for a few weeks now and formality would feel like a step backwards.
